10929-the-dog-crusoe-and-his-master-a-st:
Robert Michael Ballantyne, author of The Coral Island, wrote this prairie adventure about a dog and his young master. Dick and his dog Crusoe leave a backwoods settlement for the western plains, where buffalo hunts, Pawnee encounters, and a great feast test them. Crusoe learns his trade chapter by chapter, from puppyhood pains to guarding camp and rescuing friends.

Ballantyne fills the journey with prairie detail: buffalo wallows, foot races, Indian villages, and escapes from war parties. The dog, not the boy, is the hero of many scenes, and his loyalty drives the plot. Written for young readers in the 1890s, the book mixes adventure with the period's views of Native peoples, which modern readers should meet with a critical eye.
17334-initiative-psychic-energy-being-th:
Warren Hilton's Initiative: Psychic Energy, sixth of twelve volumes on applied psychology for personal and business efficiency, appeared in 1920 under the Literary Digest. Chapters cover mental second wind, sticking to the job, lagging brains, reserve power, blue Mondays, and how to strike one's stride. Reserves of power, genius, city life, and the threshold of inhibition follow.

Hilton writes in brisk, practical prose for workers and managers who want more drive. His terms belong to early applied psychology, yet his tips on persistence still read plain. Readers of self-help history will find a lively period manual on energy, habit, and getting started, and staying started, at work.
21081-scientific-american-volume-xliii-n:
Dated December 18, 1880, this weekly issue of Scientific American calls itself a journal of practical information, art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures. It was published in New York and cost $3.20 a year, postage prepaid. One issue shows what curious readers wanted each week.

Contents range over a new air engine, a hand-power band saw, a submarine gun, and the eruption of Mauna Loa. Shorter notes answer questions on batteries, belts, carbons, and tempering chisels. Pieces on business colleges, the Hercules beetle, and the harbour at Montreal sit side by side. It is a snapshot of invention in 1880.
21899-a-rip-van-winkle-of-the-kalahari-a:
Seven tales of South-West Africa fill Frederick Carruthers Cornell's A Rip Van Winkle of the Kalahari, published at Cape Town and London. The title story begins with a trader who crossed the Kunene River into Amboland after elephants and ivory. In German territory, where roads were few and much land unexplored, he meets a man with a wild tale. Sleep, pleasant berries, and an awakening forty years later give the story its Rip Van Winkle turn.

Other tales salt the great north-eastern fields with a prospector named Dick Sydney, walk the path of skulls, and drink the waters of Erongo. Cornell knew the desert country at first hand. His Africa is sandstorms, pans, poison flowers, and craters. The stories mix fact, yarn, and wonder in a prospector's voice.
24932-the-tribune-of-nova-scotia-a-chron:
William Lawson Grant's chronicle of Joseph Howe, published in Toronto in 1915 as volume twenty-six of the Chronicles of Canada, follows Nova Scotia's great tribune from journalist to statesman. Howe's fight for responsible government anchors the narrative: the long campaign to make colonial ministers answer to an elected assembly rather than to London's appointees. His gift for speech turned public meetings into instruments of reform.

Railways form the second thread, as Howe pressed for lines that would bind the province to its neighbors and to the wider world. Baffled hopes shadow the later chapters, when grand plans met hard politics and personal cost. Grant tells the story plainly, letting Howe's energy and disappointments carry a chapter of Canadian history that still shapes the country.
2855-elissa-or-the-doom-of-zimbabwe:
H. Rider Haggard set Elissa, or the Doom of Zimbabwe, in an ancient African city of stone, ruled from a hall of audience by Sakon, governor of Zimboe. A caravan arrives, the grove of the goddess Baaltis receives worship, and King Ithobal of the tribes takes a stormy farewell audience before departing. Elissa, a priestess figure, is caught between the rites of Baaltis and her love for Aziel.

The plot runs through dreams, sacrifice, a black dwarf, a tryst, and a cage of death, with martyrdom and sanctuary in between. Haggard again dedicates the book to the memory of Nada Burnham. The novel shows his taste for lost cities and religious conflict, told at romance speed.
29686-the-fiery-totem-a-tale-of-adventur:
Argyll Saxby, author of Braves, White and Red and Tangled Trails, wrote The Fiery Totem. It is a tale of adventure in the Canadian North-West, printed in London by the Religious Tract Society in a second impression. Its chapters open with a perilous passage and deer-stalking, then the lonely camp, friends or foes, lost in the forest, and the medicine man. A picture shows a boy gripping his weapon by the muzzle and springing straight for the pack.

Two chums worry that their parents, not they, will need care in unknown waters in a cockleshell boat. Saxby writes boys' adventure with a missionary publisher's moral frame. Young readers and fans of northern tales will find a brisk, brave story of forest, totem, and trial.
30319-beyond-the-frontier-a-romance-of-e:
Randall Parrish sets a romance of early days in the Middle West, published by A. L. Burt in New York in October 1915, by arrangement with A. C. McClurg. A frontispiece by the Kinneys shows a heroine warning a Monsieur not to doubt how her race repays insult. Chapters open at the home of Hugo Chevet, with the choice of a husband, an appeal for aid, and a scene in the palace of the intendant.

The order of La Barre, the wife of Francois Cassion, two men meeting, and a defiance of Cassion follow, with flames of jealousy and a journey to the Ottawa. Speech with De Artigny, a summit bluff, a lake, St. Ignace, and the murder of Chevet carry the tale onward, as a pledge saves De Artigny and the pair exchange confidences. Parrish, author of When Wilderness Was King, writes frontier romance with French names and action.
32310-dorothy-at-oak-knowe:
Evelyn Raymond's Dorothy book, copyrighted in 1910, sends its American heroine on the road to Oak Knowe, a new home full of fresh faces and small crises. Early chapters cover unfortunate beginnings, a party given by the Gilpins, a fright involving Millikins-Pillikins, and a visit to the Fall of the Maiden's Bath. Dorothy meets peers and commoners, neighbours and servants, and learns the manners and tempers of a new household.

The volume stands among a long series that also includes Dorothy at Skyrie, Dorothy's Schooling, Dorothy's Travels, and Dorothy on a Ranch. Its appeal lies in truthful, lively scenes of girlhood: travel, friendship, mistakes, and making good. Young readers get adventure without sensationalism, and older readers get a period picture of American family life.
33449-conduct-of-sir-william-howe:
Israel Mauduit's observations on the conduct of Sir William Howe at the White Plains, as related in the Gazette of December 30, 1776, form a sharp Revolutionary pamphlet. Reprinted in 1971 from an early edition, the tract asks whether Howe's conduct at White Plains served Britain well, in the plain, critical style of wartime debate. Its series, Eyewitness Accounts of the American Revolution, frames it as a primary source.

The pamphlet suits readers of Revolutionary history, offering a contemporary critique rather than a later historian's view. Its tone is pointed and political, aimed at readers who followed the war's conduct. For students of 1776, it is a useful, short source on how Howe's generalship was judged in his own time.
34031-raemaekers-cartoon-history-of-the-:
J. Murray Allison compiled this cartoon history of the war's first twelve months, published in New York in 1918 by the Century Company. The cartoons are by Louis Raemaekers, whose picture fronts the volume. A note singles out the Belgian cartoons to page 86, drawn long before official reports from Belgium, France, and Britain appeared.

Allison stresses that German outrages began on the evening of August 3, when troops crossed the frontier, and ran unabated until the defeat at the Marne. Only the cartoon on page 86 followed a British official report. The book preserves a sharp, wartime view of the war's first year.
britannica-1911-bancroft-hubert-howe:
Hubert Howe Bancroft (born 1832) was an American historical writer, born at Granville, Ohio, on 5 May 1832. From 1852 to 1868 he kept a bookshop in San Francisco. In those years he gathered a great library of historical material, then gave up business to publish what it held.

His Native Races of the Pacific States filled five volumes in 1874–1876, and his History of the Pacific States of North America ran to twenty-one volumes in 1882–1890. A corps of assistants gathered the data, so the books act as an encyclopaedia rather than one unified history, the entry says, but their store of material is great and lasting. The University of California bought his collection in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-troke:
John de Trokelowe was a Benedictine chronicler of St. Albans whose annals cover the reigns of Edward I and Edward II. A monk of St. Albans living at the dependent priory of Tynemouth in 1294, he was caught in the priory's bid for independence and sent back to St. Albans as a prisoner by Abbot John of Berkamsted.

There he wrote his Annals from 1259 to 1296 and a useful account of Edward II's reign from 1307 to 1323, after which Henry de Blaneford continued the chronicle. A reference to the execution of Mortimer shows he was still writing after 1330, though his birth and death dates are unknown. His work, edited by Riley in the Rolls Series, remains a valuable monastic record of troubled years in church and kingdom.
doe-osti-2583502-dynamic-model-developme: Wind plant forecasting with neural nets got its CRADA final, and this report covers the dynamic model development. The pages record the predictions. The wind operators get their forecaster. The method was neural net. The output was wind power. The operators got forecasters.
doe-osti-3000825-a-novel-manufacturing-p: Lightweight car seats got a novel process, and this DOE text mixes additive manufacturing with reinforcement. The pages detail the findings. The auto folks get their method. The seats were lightweight automotive. The method was auto. The reinforcement was integrated.
doe-osti-3000902-building-resiliency-int: Grand Canyon West got its resilient micro-grid, and this DOE text builds the resiliency in. The pages detail the design. The tribal energy folks get their playbook. The grid was micro. The playbook was tribal energy. The design was detailed.
doe-osti-3002955-a-novel-manufacturing-p: Lightweight car seats got a novel process, and this DOE text mixes additive manufacturing with reinforcement. The pages detail the findings. The auto folks get their method. The seats were lightweight automotive. The method was auto. The reinforcement was integrated.
doe-osti-3022545-highly-recyclable-therm: Tough plastics getting a second life got their DOE green recipe, and this text bakes the lightweight mix. The pages detail the composite results. The materials folks get their data. The recipe was thermoset. The mix was lightweight. The recipe was green.
doe-osti-3097912-qualitative-risk-assess: Legacy wells got risk-assessed, and this DOE text covers Prairie State review. The pages detail the qualitative findings. The energy folks get their data. The area was generating company. The data were energy. The State were Prairie. The review were area.
doe-osti-3412942-entanglement-informed-t: Quantum computers come in different flavors — adiabatic machines and gate-based optimizers among them. Quiroz and Titum develop entanglement-informed translations between AQC and QAOA, mapping problems from one style to the other. The translations let researchers pick the right quantum tool for each job.
elissa-or-the-doom-of-zimbabwe:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this novella to rebuild the lost Phoenician city behind the ruins of Great Zimbabwe in Rhodesia. His note in the text admits the evidence is scant: old workings, vast walls, and temples to Phoenician gods. The story he builds on them is headed by Elissa, priestess of the Baaltis, the goddess of the city.

Prince Aziel, a Jewish prince come with a trading caravan, plights his troth where the city's faith forbids it. King Ithobal, the prophet Issachar, and the merchant Metem fill out the court. Sacrilege, martyrdom, sanctuary, and the cage of death mark the chapters as the surrounding tribes close in. Haggard first printed the tale in his 1900 volume Black Heart and White Heart, and Other Stories; this hosted text keeps that volume's dedication and author's note.
govdocs-archive_org-montauk-the-alien-co:
Montauk: The Alien Connection tells the story of Stewart Swerdlow, a man who said his extrasensory abilities drew him into secret government work. It belongs to the Montauk literature, the body of claims that grew up around alleged experiments at Montauk, Long Island.

Swerdlow describes being watched and used for his mental gifts, then deprogrammed with the help of Preston Nichols, a central figure in the Montauk stories. He also tells of being jailed after refusing to cut his ties with Nichols. The book is presented as an archive holding, a first-person account at the heart of the Montauk myth.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrazierBuellWes:
A manuscript titled The Bag, most likely by Harold Weisberg, takes up the paper bag in the Kennedy case and Buell Wesley Frazier. Frazier was the young man who drove Lee Harvey Oswald to work on the morning of the assassination. The bag was the package Oswald was said to have carried that day.

Few objects in the case carry more argument per ounce. Whether the bag held a rifle, and how it was handled, shaped the case against Oswald. A manuscript devoted to it shows Weisberg's method: one piece of evidence, examined until it gives up its problems.
initiative-psychic-energy-being-the-sixt:
Warren Hilton wrote Initiative Psychic Energy as the sixth of twelve volumes on applied psychology. The Society of Applied Psychology issued it in New York in 1920. Chapters promise a mental second wind and ways to stick to the job. Blue Mondays, stored energies, and the lawyer who overworks are treated.

Tests of hearing with an acoumeter appear in a middle section on mental friction. Hilton urges readers to stop wasting energy in haphazard ways. Reserves of power, he argues, can be released by desire and habit. The book belongs to the early self-help and business efficiency movement.
lucan-pharsalia-rowe:
Lucan, a young Roman poet under Nero, wrote the Pharsalia on Caesar's civil war. Nicholas Rowe's translation presents the unfinished epic in English couplets. Lucan died by Nero's order at twenty-five, leaving ten books.

The poem follows Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon and Pompey's fall. Cato becomes its moral hero, dying nobly rather than submitting to tyranny. Lucan drops the gods and fills the space with rhetoric and horror. Witches, deserts, and sea battles crowd his verses. Rowe, himself a playwright, drives the story forward energetically. The epic reads Rome's tragedy as the death of liberty itself.
podcast-joerogan-EhU-yzauNWE:
Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1596. Loeb made headlines by arguing that an interstellar object that passed our system might be alien technology. Most of his peers disagreed, which is exactly why his case draws a crowd.

He explains the object's odd path and shine, and why he thinks a natural rock does not fit. Rogan asks about the pushback Loeb took from other scientists and his project to hunt for more such visitors. The episode is a famous scientist's heresy stated calmly, and a lesson in how science fights over its edges.
podcast-tuckercarlson-3Wi_zQX--wE:
An economist joins Tucker Carlson to advance a sweeping thesis: every major war begins under false pretenses, and central banks stand behind the pattern. The guest walks through the claim war by war, arguing that the stated causes of conflicts rarely match the financial interests that profit from them.

Carlson, long skeptical of American wars, presses for the mechanism: who lends, who gains, and how the story sold to the public gets built. The argument echoes an old tradition of war criticism that runs through American history. Listeners get the strongest version of it here, from a guest who treats banking as the hidden constant of modern conflict. The episode is kept as the argument was made, for audiences to test against the record.
the-dog-crusoe-and-his-master-a-story-of:
Robert Michael Ballantyne's The Dog Crusoe and His Master, subtitled A Story of Adventure in the Western Prairies, is dated 1894. Its contents run from Crusoe's puppyhood and a shooting match to his training and a mission of peace. The title page lists Ballantyne's other boys' books, among them The Coral Island, Ungava, and Martin Rattler.

Dick, the young master, and Crusoe cross the plains on hunts and errands among Native peoples and traders. Ballantyne packs the tale with camp craft and close calls. It stands as a prime case of Victorian boys' adventure writing.
